Launching Harness Comparisons on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index: the best harness varies between models, and harness choice has a greater impact on cost than score

Harness Comparisons hold the model fixed and change only the harness, to show how the harness affects a model's performance. We ran 
@OpenAI
's GPT-6 Luna and 
@Zai_org
's GLM-5.3-Flash at max reasoning effort in 13 harnesses each, across v2.1 of the Coding Agent Index.

Key takeaways:

➤ No single harness is best across models: performance depends on the harness and model as a pair. GPT-6 Luna scores highest in Codex (26), OpenAI's own harness, which ranks last with GLM-5.3-Flash. GLM-5.3-Flash scores highest in Claude Code (39), which ranks 6th with GPT-6 Luna

➤ The harnesses that offer the best performance per dollar differ by model: with GPT-6 Luna they are Pi (21 at $0.11 per task), mini-swe-agent (25 at $0.16) and Codex (26 at $0.19). With GLM-5.3-Flash they are Mistral Vibe (37 at $0.38), Kimi Code CLI (37 at $0.56) and Claude Code (39 at $0.58). No harness is on the Pareto frontier for both models

➤ The harness has a greater impact on cost than score: 11 of 13 harnesses score 20 to 26 with GPT-6 Luna and 10 of 13 score 35 to 39 with GLM-5.3-Flash. Cost per task ranges from $0.11 in Pi to $0.62 in Muse Code with GPT-6 Luna, and from $0.38 in Mistral Vibe to $0.91 in Devin CLI with GLM-5.3-Flash

➤ GLM-5.3-Flash reasons differently inside Codex: it reasons in terse fragments in Codex and in full prose in the other 12 harnesses, and produces 52k output tokens per task in Codex, compared with 97k to 202k elsewhere. We believe this contributes to its lowest performance occurring in the Codex harness

Octen Search (fast, dynamic) returns each search in ~0.17s, the fastest of the 25 Search API products we benchmark, and scores 82 on the Artificial Analysis Search Index

We benchmarked the fast, dynamic mode of 
@OctenAI
's Search API in our Stirrup agent harness with Octen Search as its web_search tool to complete 1700 search-focused tasks.

In our September run, Octen Search (highlights) scored 77. In these November runs, Octen Search (fast, dynamic) scores 82.

Key benchmarking results for Octen Search:

➤ Speed: each search returns in about 0.17s, the lowest of the 25 Search API products and about half the next lowest (0.33s). Time per Task is 13.3s, the lowest of 26 and comparable to Parallel Search (fast, objective) (14.3s) and Keenable Search (realtime) (14.4s), against a board median of about 26s

➤ Artificial Analysis Search Index: 82, 3rd of 26, within 1 point of Parallel Search (advanced, objective) and Keenable Search (pro) at 83. That is a ~49-point lift over the same model with no search (33). No product scores higher in less time

➤ BrowseComp: Octen scores 92% on our hard BrowseComp subset (200 questions), the highest of 26 and ~4 points above Keenable Search (pro) and Perplexity Search (medium) at 87%. Octen scores 84 F1 on DeepSearchQA (7th) and 72% on AA-Omniscience (joint 6th)

➤ Low cost: about $0.018 per task, 3rd lowest of 26 behind TinyFish ($0.009) and Parallel Search (fast, objective) ($0.014), against a board median of $0.063

Key details:

➤ Setup: GPT-5.6 Luna (medium) in Stirrup, Octen Search API with result_type=dynamic

➤ Dynamic results: Octen returns only the results it finds relevant, up to the 10 we request, and sets the highlight length for each result

➤ Pricing: $1 per 1k requests

tl;dr of the article is AI just solved the riemann hypothesis while no human could, and it's way harder than most of our industries' problems, so we have superintelligence

tbh i don't buy this, and here's why - 

LLMs we have today are trained through two stages: pre-training and post-training. if you want a simple mental model - pre-training teaches wisdom, and post-training teaches behaviors

solving the riemann hypothesis is proof that our pre-training is already quite incredible, although i think even there we still have a lot more to do in terms of multi-modality and physical world modeling

post-training however is quite a mess. i explained in many of my previous tweets the limitations of the current RLVR pipelines. it's why the same AI that can solve riemann hypothesis would still produce useless comments, bad test cases, and slop writing etc etc

what we have is something highly intelligent in theory, but still suck at many real world tasks, because the behaviors required to do well in those tasks had to be taught one by one

agentic coding, browser use, computer use, 3d modeling - each skill had to be trained in the labs through predefined RL environments. the models can't really learn these skills on the fly like how a 16yr-old human can learn how to drive with just a few days

it doesn't look like we already have these fundamental problems figured out yet. and it's unclear that being able to solve the riemann hypothesis proves there are viable solutions to these unknowns

all in all, i think what we have is already super exciting, but it's still early to say we have superintelligence figured out. what do you think? do you feel you have superintelligence at hand?

i'm now pretty convinced that one of the most important metrics to watch out for in your codebases when most work is done by agents is -

median $ cost per task

this screenshot is one of my recent codebases which grew from 100k to 1M lines of code over the past month from intense development

the median $ cost of a task kept growing as well. and each time i noticed it was rising, i did some analysis to understand why, and did optimizations to drive it back down

my task cost is actually pretty high because the repo is a cross-platform app and most features need to work on mac, linux, windows, and mobile

i'm reasonably happy that the cost only rose by 70% when the codebase is now 10x complexity. it wouldn't have been possible without lots of optimizations, because agents by default don't care about long term maintainability (explained in a previous tweet)

if i had left it unchecked, every task would have become a lot slower and more costly, and i wouldn't have been able to keep the pace of development

a prompt you can use to start understanding what's happening with your work -

"look at my past month's agent sessions' usage stats in this codebase to calculate a 7d sliding window median $ cost per task and report it as a chart"
